title: Account 4471
logline: When a trafficked worker in a border scam compound inherits a six-month romance account, the lonely American on the other end has already worked out that the photographs are stolen but stays for the mind behind them, and the two men keep the fiction going until a collapse forces a meeting in which the messages the American loved most turn out to have been written by someone else.

scenes.beat: Supervisor Lee assigns Sam the account of 'Grace Lin', a persona whose conversation with an American named Paul Whitaker is flagged CONVERSION OVERDUE on the dashboard. Sam must read the whole six-month archive before he is allowed to type, while a beating goes on in the next room and no one stops working. He decides the previous operator misunderstood Paul, who is lonely for argument and not for romance, since she answered his 2,000-word essay on lighthouse keepers with three heart emojis. Sam's contempt for the earlier writer becomes the first private feeling he has had in weeks.

Sam studies the persona guidelines (commas and hearts, never semicolons, QA flags every violation) and catalogues the previous operator's tells, which he thinks of as Ana's: she opens a thought with 'hm,' she spells 'grey' the British way, and she signs off long letters with a lowercase 'ok?'. He finds her masterpiece in month three, a letter about a ferry crossing and a grandmother's kitchen, with Paul's reply saying he has printed it and pinned it above his desk. Sam sees that Ana's hand vanishes after month four. He now has a rival he can study but cannot question.

On his first live shift Paul asks for help with a sentence in the harbour-pilot manual he is translating, and Sam, without meaning to, answers in Grace's voice with a true memory of his own mother saving the heels of bread for the birds. Paul replies within a minute, delighted, and asks 'Who are you tonight?' Sam's message contains one semicolon that he typed without noticing. QA flags it, Lee logs the first violation against him, and Paul screenshots the message and keeps it.

A week in, Paul has deposited nothing and Lee reviews the ratio on the wall monitor. He puts Sam on a performance improvement plan and starts an A/B test: Grace confides a debt crisis to Paul under Variant B, 'vulnerability first'. Sam sends the softened script. Paul answers with a consolidation plan, a link to a credit counsellor and no money, and the plan is so kind and so useless that Sam's supervisor circles the word 'counsellor' in red.

Ben, the worker at the next desk, misses his quota and is taken to the next room, and the office keeps typing to the sound of it. Afterwards Sam understands that his own PIP has a date on it. He starts writing Paul longer, more intellectual messages to keep him engaged and keep the score alive, and one of them is flagged 'too emotionally reciprocal'. He has begun to protect the conversation and can no longer separate that from protecting himself.

Paul reverse-image-searches Grace's photographs and finds them on the profile of a dental hygienist in another country, and he understands that the woman he loves does not exist in those pictures. He does not confront. He writes, 'What can you see from where you're sitting? I mean literally.' Sam cannot lie about himself, so he answers truthfully: a wall the colour of old teeth, a fan that ticks, and a river he can hear but not see. Paul thanks him and asks for more, and both men understand that the other knows.

acts.title: Act Two: Two Hands, One Voice

scenes.beat: Ana comes back from a month in another building, thinner, and Lee sets her up as night operator on Grace with Sam on days, so the account is now run by two people who are told to hide the seam. Reading Sam's logs, Ana tells him flatly that he has made Grace remember things she cannot, and she knows the ferry letter better than he does. From that night the archive has two authors on purpose, and Sam is the one who has to learn her rules.

Sam hides a plea inside a message to Paul, an acrostic spelling HELP down the first letters of the lines, and Ana sees the draft and lets it pass. Paul, proud of his mind, notices the pattern and replies with a long essay on apophenia and why humans find words in coincidence, and he never considers that this one is real. Sam's cleverness dies against Paul's cleverness, and the hidden plea is now spent.

Lee orders an emergency script: Grace is in hospital and needs $6,000 within 24 hours. Ana writes it and Sam has to send it. Paul does not pay. He asks for the hospital's name and a city, says he will fly out, and leaves the request open. Lee sees a live visitor and assigns Sam to give Paul a meeting point where a broker will collect him. The con becomes a kidnapping plan, and the account that has never produced a deposit now looks worth more to Lee than any deposit.

Paul writes to the real dental hygienist to ask if she knows her photographs are being used, and she answers with fury, posts his name in a victims' forum, and his message history reaches a friend. Paul is humiliated in public by a woman who owes him nothing. At 2:40 in the morning, compound time, he returns to Grace and writes, 'I was told I'm an idiot today. Are you still there?'

The 3 AM conversation: Paul asks whether Kierkegaard's leap of faith has to leap toward anything, and Sam, working through translation software and a summary he memorised, defends the knight of faith and misquotes 'Fear and Trembling' so badly that Paul corrects him and laughs. All night the dashboard cycles CONVERSION OVERDUE in red and Lee's messages pile up. At 4:10 two guards take Sam to the next room for a missed quota, and Ana slides into his chair and writes the closing lines in Grace's voice: 'hm. If it's a leap, someone has to be on the other side. I'll be here, in whatever way here means.' Paul answers, 'That's the one.' Sam returns bleeding, reads the exchange, and learns that the night he thought was his was finished by the rival he envies.

In the dormitory Ana tells Sam she took the chair because she could not stand to hear Paul wait. She admits she wrote the ferry letter from her own grandmother's kitchen, and Sam says nothing about his mother. Lee announces that Paul's flight is booked for Friday, five days away, and that the account will be harvested. Sam and Ana agree that the account cannot end with Paul at the meeting point, and they decide Sam will write the next message alone in plain words.

Sam writes Paul without a script: 'Do not come. Do not send anything. There are two hundred of us in a building by a river, and the wall is the colour of old teeth.' He sends it before QA can flag it, and Lee reads the log an hour later and drags him to the next room. Paul, this time, reads the message as it is, and forwards the account logs, the window description, and every timestamp to a tip line and a journalist. He writes Grace only, 'I did something. I'm not coming.'

On Thursday the gate is opened from outside. The power dies mid-alert and the dashboard freezes on CONVERSION OVERDUE while supervisors leave with the cash boxes and the crowd runs for the river road. Ana pulls the archive drive from Lee's tower, presses it into Sam's hands, and goes back into the building for a friend. Sam crosses the river with the drive and cannot tell whether she is behind him.

Months later, in a repatriation office in a city far from the river, Paul meets Sam for the first time. Paul has brought his folder: the ferry letter, the semicolon message, and the printout of 'hm. If it's a leap, someone has to be on the other side.' He tells Sam that these are the pages he loved most, and that he knew Sam by the grandmother's kitchen. Sam tells him the ferry letter was Ana's, the closing lines were Ana's, and only the semicolon was his own. Paul realises he has never spoken to the person he came to meet as one person, and asks for Ana's real name. Sam writes it on the back of the ferry letter, in his own handwriting, which Paul has never seen.
